mappings.note: Which compound escapes systematic prefix naming (NH3, called ammonia). A nomenclature convention question, so LO-42's 'scientific conventions' clause. No formula is derived, so the valency half of LO-42 and all of LO-41 are idle.

The MCQ form of the neon item 6a44cb5e, and the same outcome: a filled valence shell means no compound forms. Stated plainly rather than manufactured - the frame has one formation outcome and no way to separate a two-mark written answer from a one-mark MCQ on the same idea.

How sodium reaches stability when bonding with chlorine: it donates its single valence electron. Formation of an ionic compound, LO-40. The resulting charge is a by-product, not the demand, so LO-41 is not cited.

Bare terminology: name the electrostatic force between oppositely charged ions. LO-48's 'different types of bonding (ionic and covalent)' at the familiarity level C7.1 explicitly allows. LO-40 is kept for items where the bond is formed or explained rather than merely named.
Crossover of valency 3 and 2 to give M2(XY4)3, bracket included. LO-42, the frame's formula-writing outcome; the valencies come off the diagram so nothing is calculated.

The false assertion is that NaCl exists as discrete molecular units. Answering it means telling an ionic lattice apart from a molecular substance - LO-39's 'differentiate ... ionic and covalent compounds' by structure. Not LO-40, which would need the lattice to be built from electron transfer, as sibling 3f16accb does.

Spot the wrong naming rule (anion written first). A convention question about ionic nomenclature, LO-42. Distinct from the prefix items only in subject matter, not in outcome - the frame has one naming home.

Recall the sulfate ion's formula and its valency of 2 from the polyatomic-ion table. LO-42's 'symbols and valency' clause. Explicitly not LO-41, whose valency clause is 'valency from the atomic number', which cannot be applied to a polyatomic ion at all.
The four-step procedure for writing an ionic formula, with a bogus 'multiply by two' step planted. Method knowledge for LO-42, not an application of it to a specific compound like 064bf271.
Al2O3 from valencies 3 and 2, with AlO and Al3O2 as traps. LO-42 applied to a named compound - the companion procedural item ba586aaa tests the same outcome as a rule list.

Why the bracket in Al(OH)3 is required: the subscript must apply to the whole polyatomic group. LO-42's convention clause; the item explains a convention rather than producing a formula, but there is no other outcome covering formula notation.

Equal valencies cross to Ca2(CO3)2 and must be reduced to CaCO3. The simplification rule is part of LO-42's formula conventions; the reduction is not a mass or charge calculation, so LO-41 does not apply.

Camphor and naphthalene are insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents. Classifying covalent compounds by a physical property is LO-39's differentiation clause; C1.2 was considered for the solvent angle but its content is separation techniques and mixture types, not covalent solubility.

Why an ionic solid does not conduct - ions fixed in the lattice. A single-species property explanation, mapped to LO-39 because the frame's only property-bearing outcome is LO-39's 'differentiate ... based on their properties or characteristics'. A mildly loose fit: nothing is actually compared here.
Assertion and reason both about free ions in aqueous NaCl carrying charge. Property-based characterisation of an ionic compound, LO-39, with no formation or calculation in the item.
Sugar dissolves yet does not conduct. The item exists to contrast a molecular solute with an ionic one, which is LO-39's ionic-versus-covalent differentiation in its sharpest form.

High melting and boiling points traced to strong inter-ionic attraction. Property-based characterisation, LO-39. Its part-6 long-form relative d3a6bcf9 makes the ionic/covalent comparison explicit and shares the outcome.

Two separate demands: predicting that a two-valence-electron metal transfers to oxygen and forms an ionic bond is LO-40, and predicting that the solution conducts is the property half, LO-39. Its part-1 sibling 779e070a asks for the formula instead and picks up LO-42 rather than LO-40.
HNO3 molecular mass as an MCQ - the same computation as f13401ee, and the same outcome. LO-41 names molecular mass directly; the verbose stem changes nothing about the demand.

Ordering the three steps for a covalent formula: symbols, valencies, crossover. LO-42's method clause, and the covalent/ionic distinction does not move it, because LO-42 covers 'simple compounds' generally.

Sequencing H2 formation: approach, share, duplet complete, bond established. Mechanism, LO-40. The chlorine and oxygen sequencing items map the same way; the frame offers no outcome that distinguishes a single from a double bond.

A four-statement omnibus spanning conservation of mass, the 1:8 ratio, Dalton's indestructible atoms and the covalent-bond definition. This is the one item in the chapter where LO-48's fused four-clause row is the right code rather than a compromise: the item deliberately spans all of it and no single sibling outcome can decide it.
Who proposed the law and what it says - naming and stating, nothing more. LO-48 at the familiarity end of C7.1. Its explain-with-an-example counterpart 286c6b21 goes to LO-40 instead.
Why the open flask loses mass. The two-mark distillation of the whole apparent-violation family, LO-49; there is no procedure to design (LO-39) and no law to state (LO-48).

What you would observe when the two solutions are mixed in a closed container - white precipitate, mass unchanged. The 'observe' half of LO-39's fused verification clause; nothing is calculated and no violation is alleged.
